options.A: At least seven days

caseContext: Section A | Questions 4-6 A 59-year-old woman has type 2 diabetes and albuminuric CKD. Two weeks after starting losartan, creatinine rises from 100 to 119 micromol/L. Potassium is 4.5 mmol/L and BP is 126/76 mmHg. She is eating and drinking normally, has no orthostasis and takes no NSAIDs. Her other medicines are metformin and empagliflozin.
question: What is the best response to this creatinine change?

options.A: Add ramipril to improve albuminuria
options.B: Arrange emergency dialysis
options.C: Give IV fluids despite normal volume status
options.D: Stop losartan permanently because any rise indicates injury
options.E: Continue losartan and monitor kidney function and potassium

explanation:
Why this fits: A small early creatinine rise can reflect the expected hemodynamic effect of RAAS blockade. A 19% rise without hypovolemia or hyperkalemia usually permits continuation. 
Why the alternatives fall short: A rise above 30% warrants investigation; this result is below that threshold. Dual ACE-inhibitor/ARB therapy adds harm. 
Prescribing / safety pearl: Interpret a laboratory change with volume status, medicines and the timing of treatment.

caseContext: Section A | Questions 7-9 A 34-year-old woman uses budesonide/formoterol twice daily with salbutamol as needed. She reports symptoms most days and wakes with wheeze twice weekly. She refills the controller about half as often as expected. In clinic, she actuates the inhaler before beginning to inhale. There is no acute respiratory distress.
question: What should happen before increasing long-term treatment intensity?

options.A: Add maintenance oral prednisone immediately
options.B: Stop inhaled corticosteroid because it has failed
options.C: Add two different LABAs
options.D: Replace the controller with salbutamol alone
options.E: Check and correct technique, adherence and relevant exposures

explanation:
Why this fits: Poor adherence and ineffective technique can mimic refractory asthma. Correct these modifiable problems before assuming the prescribed dose is inadequate. 
Why the alternatives fall short: Long-term systemic steroids carry substantial toxicity. Removing the ICS or duplicating LABAs does not address the cause of poor control. 
Prescribing / safety pearl: Ask the patient to demonstrate inhaler use rather than simply asking whether technique is correct.

Prescribing / safety pearl: Write product-specific doses and the maximum daily inhalations in the action plan.

caseContext: Section A | Questions 10-12 An 83-year-old woman with nonvalvular atrial fibrillation weighs 58 kg. Serum creatinine is 110 micromol/L, calculated creatinine clearance is 32 mL/min and hemoglobin is stable. She has no active bleeding, mechanical valve or rheumatic mitral stenosis. Anticoagulation is indicated.
question: Which apixaban dose is appropriate for stroke prevention in this patient?

options.A: 2.5 mg twice daily
options.B: 5 mg twice daily regardless of age and weight
options.C: 10 mg twice daily indefinitely
options.D: 5 mg once daily
options.E: 2.5 mg once daily

explanation:
Why this fits: She meets two AF dose-reduction criteria: age at least 80 and body weight at most 60 kg. The indicated reduced dose is 2.5 mg twice daily. 
Why the alternatives fall short: The AF dosing rule differs from acute VTE treatment. Once-daily schedules are incorrect for apixaban. 
Prescribing / safety pearl: Use the correct indication-specific dose criteria and assess creatinine clearance.

options.C: A 14-day optimized bismuth quadruple regimen

explanation:
Why this fits: After failed clarithromycin triple therapy, optimized bismuth quadruple therapy is an appropriate salvage option when not previously used.

caseContext: Section A | Questions 16-18 A 51-year-old man has taken lithium for bipolar disorder for six years. Chlorthalidone was added ten days ago. question: Which recent factor most directly increases lithium retention?

options.A: A stable dietary protein intake
options.B: A saline nasal spray
options.C: Acetaminophen taken once at a normal dose
options.D: An inhaled corticosteroid
options.E: Chlorthalidone combined with volume depletion

explanation:
Why this fits: Thiazide-type diuretics and dehydration reduce lithium clearance. The neurologic findings and AKI strongly suggest clinically important toxicity. 
Why the alternatives fall short: The old therapeutic level does not describe his current exposure. The other listed products do not explain this acute retention pattern. 
Prescribing / safety pearl: Check interactions whenever a patient taking lithium receives a new prescription.

Why the alternatives fall short: Treating tremor alone misses systemic toxicity. Unmonitored forced diuresis can worsen the problem. 
Prescribing / safety pearl: Clinical toxicity can matter even when a measured level seems less dramatic than expected.

options.A: Allopurinol as the only acute analgesic
options.B: Daily ketorolac injections for one week
options.C: Standard-dose colchicine while continuing clarithromycin
options.D: A short course of oral prednisone
options.E: High-dose naproxen

explanation:
Why this fits: A short corticosteroid course avoids the major NSAID risks and the hazardous colchicine interaction in this patient. 
Why the alternatives fall short: CKD and prior ulcer bleeding increase NSAID harm. Clarithromycin plus renal impairment can cause severe colchicine toxicity. Allopurinol does not provide rapid anti-inflammatory relief. 
Prescribing / safety pearl: An intra-articular steroid can also be considered for a suitable single joint after infection is excluded.

caseContext: Section A | Questions 22-24 A 31-year-old woman at 26 weeks of pregnancy has an ultrasound-confirmed proximal DVT. She is hemodynamically stable, weighs 74 kg and has normal renal function and platelet count. She has no bleeding or heparin allergy and plans to breastfeed.
question: Which treatment is preferred during pregnancy?

options.A: Warfarin throughout pregnancy
options.B: Apixaban
options.C: Aspirin alone
options.D: Prophylactic-dose heparin despite a confirmed proximal DVT
options.E: Therapeutic weight-based low-molecular-weight heparin

explanation:
Why this fits: Therapeutic LMWH is preferred for most pregnancy-associated VTE. It does not cross the placenta. 
Why the alternatives fall short: Warfarin can harm the fetus, DOACs are generally avoided, and prophylactic dosing is inadequate for established DVT. 
Prescribing / safety pearl: Coordinate anticoagulation and delivery planning with obstetric and thrombosis teams.

caseContext: Section A | Questions 22-24 A 31-year-old woman at 26 weeks of pregnancy has an ultrasound-confirmed proximal DVT. She is hemodynamically stable, weighs 74 kg and has normal renal function and platelet count. She has no bleeding or heparin allergy and plans to breastfeed.

options.C: Edoxaban as the routine default
options.D: Rivaroxaban without individualized review

Prescribing / safety pearl: If changing from LMWH to warfarin, arrange appropriate overlap and INR monitoring.

caseContext: Section A | Questions 22-24 A 31-year-old woman at 26 weeks of pregnancy has an ultrasound-confirmed proximal DVT. She is hemodynamically stable, weighs 74 kg and has normal renal function and platelet count. She has no bleeding or heparin allergy and plans to breastfeed.

caseContext: Section A | Questions 25-27 An 86-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes, moderate dementia and CKD has repeated fasting glucose readings of 2.8-3.4 mmol/L. A1c is 6.2%. question: Which medication change is the priority?

options.A: Add mealtime insulin
options.B: Increase glyburide to maintain A1c below 6%
options.C: Stop or deintensify glyburide promptly and reassess the regimen
options.D: Add a second sulfonylurea
options.E: Treat only with a larger bedtime snack indefinitely

explanation:
Why this fits: Recurrent hypoglycemia in a frail patient outweighs the benefit of very tight glycemic control. Glyburide can cause prolonged hypoglycemia, especially in CKD. 
Why the alternatives fall short: More insulin secretagogue or insulin increases immediate risk. Snacks alone do not correct an unsafe regimen. 
Prescribing / safety pearl: Review renal appropriateness of every remaining medicine, including metformin.

caseContext: Section A | Questions 25-27 An 86-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes, moderate dementia and CKD has repeated fasting glucose readings of 2.8-3.4 mmol/L. A1c is 6.2%. Why the alternatives fall short: An isolated moderate reading is not a reason for aggressive escalation in this context. Monitoring still helps guide safe deintensification. 
Prescribing / safety pearl: Include the caregiver and simplify dosing whenever possible.

caseContext: Section A | Questions 57-58 A 42-year-old woman with primary adrenal insufficiency has vomiting and cannot retain her usual hydrocortisone. She is weak and confused, BP is 78/46 mmHg, sodium is 126 mmol/L, potassium is 5.7 mmol/L and glucose is 3.1 mmol/L. IV access is available.

caseContext: Section A | Questions 59-60 A 25-year-old woman started recommended outpatient ceftriaxone, doxycycline and metronidazole for pelvic inflammatory disease. caseContext: Section B | Questions 77-79 A 28-year-old woman with epilepsy had her lamotrigine dose increased during pregnancy to maintain seizure control as levels fell. caseContext: Section B | Questions 135-136 A 30-year-old woman at 11 weeks of pregnancy has hemoglobin 101 g/L, ferritin 7 micrograms/L and microcytosis. She is stable without bleeding or cardiopulmonary symptoms. She can tolerate oral medication and has no evidence of malabsorption.
